item.title: A Billion More Dark-Morning Commutes
item.description:
Sleep

A Billion More Dark-Morning Commutes

How permanent daylight saving time would affect students.

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • If permanent daylight saving time were adopted, darker winter mornings would affect students.
  • More time waiting for buses would be in the dark and more commutes by car or bus would be in the dark.
  • Concerns about student safety are paramount in opposition to permanent daylight saving time.
Source: Joseph A. Buckhalt/No Copyright

In July, my post about the big debate over yearly time changes described the position of professional sleep organizations that permanent standard time (ST) is more aligned with our circadian physiology than permanent daylight saving time (DST), or the alternating system we currently have in the U.S. (except in Arizona). As a member of one of those organizations, and having read their arguments, I am in favor of permanent standard time.

Since I posted, an interesting study was released to journalists on October 29, which estimated the number of dark-morning student-commutes to school we would see if the “Sunshine Protection Act” (proposing permanent DST) had been passed by the Senate and signed into law. Rodríguez Ferrante and colleagues at the University of Washington calculated that the number was around a billion. Central to their argument against permanent DST was their analysis of a decade of national fatal crash records, which found that there were higher odds of pedestrian involvement in dark-morning crashes than light-morning ones (odds ratio [OR] 1.77), and even higher odds for children aged 5–18 (OR 2.22). Safety for children waiting for the bus and riding to school in buses and cars was a primary concern of some senators.

How have you and your family adjusted to this fall's time change? As for myself, after four days, I still get sleepy earlier in the evening and wake up earlier. I am in the “elderly” demographic, and it seems that with older age comes slower adjustment by the circadian clock (Lombardi, 2025). Lombardi explains that infants and older persons have a harder time adjusting to time changes, and the article also describes the physiology that makes adjustment difficult for many of us. Typically "spring foward" is more difficult for evening types (owls) than for morning types (larks), since they have to adjust to getting up earlier.

I came across an interesting fact in an American history book. It stated that “On Tuesday, October 30, 1787, readers of a newspaper, the New York Packet, found on the front page an advertisement for an almanac that came bound with tables predicting the 'Rising and Setting of the Sun,' the 'Judgement of the Weather,' the 'Length of Days and Nights’…” (Lepore, 2018, p.xi.). This was, of course, Ben Franklin’s Poor Richard’s Almanac. And while other almanacs with such information were available in early America, Franklin’s was the most read secular book of the time (the Bible was first overall). It is interesting to ponder what Franklin would have thought about changing the clocks and which of the three most discussed alternatives he might have supported. Among his inventions was a clock, and I have no doubt that he could have altered it to automatically adjust for yearly time changes.

item.title: Postpartum Prevention Plan: Time Outside, Exercise, Socialize
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

Postpartum Prevention Plan: Time Outside, Exercise, Socialize

Three research-backed tips to prevent the baby blues.

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • Nature has benefits for postnatal mood, emotional regulation, optimism, resilience, and child development.
  • A meta-analysis found exercise alone can be effective in reducing postpartum depression and anxiety.
  • Social support is a powerful protective factor in preventing postpartum depression and anxiety.
  • Some postpartum symptoms are resistant to lifestyle changes and remit with professional treatment.

Postpartum depression and anxiety are major issues that affect new caregivers. Many new parents focus on the birth plan to prepare for this major stage of life. But what I find in my work as a clinical psychologist is that new families really benefit from a postpartum plan as well. What are the needs, relationships, and activities that will help you maintain your well-being postpartum? Knowing these will promote your child’s well-being as well. I developed the following mnemonic to capture core helpful practices that are supported by research: Time Outside, Exercise, and Socialize. These three practices can provide a daily structure that maximizes joy during a time that is challenging but also fulfilling.

Postpartum Prevention Plan

1. Time Outside: Follow the mantra often told to caregivers of newborns — leave the house every day. Time spent in nature has been associated with enhanced mood, emotional regulation, optimism, resilience, and child development (Hall et al., 2023). Research on mothers and nature has attested to the benefits of the outdoors on postnatal well-being and the relief it provides from indoor stressors (Hall et al., 2023). Getting out is key. Even if being in nature isn't possible, go out for coffee, lunch, or to a museum to provide novelty and stimulation that can vary your routine and perk up the day. Physicians have dispelled myths that you shouldn’t leave home with your newborn, as fresh air and a change of scenery are beneficial to both parent and child well-being (Davis, 2015).

2. Exercise: If you are able to, getting some kind of walk in every day with a newborn is not only good for you but also for your child. Strap them into a carrier of your choosing or affix a stroller with all the things you might need to leave the house for an hour. A meta-analysis reviewing a wide range of studies found that exercise alone (without the use of other interventions) is effective in reducing postpartum depression and anxiety (Deprato et al., 2025). A moderate reduction in the severity of symptoms was achieved through at least 80 minutes a week of rigorous exercise, which could include a brisk walk, swimming, cycling, and other activities.

3. Socialize: Invite a friend or family member for a visit or walk. Attend a local baby-friendly gathering that can take you and an infant out into the world, like a yoga, music, play, or story time group. Research suggests that social interaction is a powerful protective factor in preventing postpartum depression and anxiety (Feinberg et al., 2022). Another study found that social support is particularly important for women who are at risk of postpartum mental health problems, such as those with more than one child, pregnancy loss, negative body image, and a history of mental health problems.

It is important to note that all three of these components overlap — socializing, time outside, and exercise could all take place during a long walk with a friend. But if you are having trouble getting out with the baby, have others help you, if possible, so you don’t have to make this happen on your own. And if consistent practice of these activities doesn’t seem to help, reaching out to a medical and/or mental health professional is essential. Severe cases of postpartum depression and anxiety may be resistant to daily health behaviors, but professional treatment is still effective. More support is available at the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline (1-833-852-6262) and Postpartum Support International (1-800-944-4773).

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
